opus-5.5.text:
I think the best way to understand AlphaEvolve's generality is to look at what it actually needs from you. The core requirement is surprisingly simple: you need a problem whose solution can be expressed as code, and you need a way to automatically evaluate how good a candidate solution is. If you have those two things, the system can, in principle, go to work.

That's a very different kind of generality from what we had with something like AlphaFold. AlphaFold was built for one extraordinarily important problem, predicting protein structure, and a lot of domain knowledge went into its design. AlphaEvolve is more of a general-purpose discovery engine. It pairs the creativity of large language models, the Gemini models, which propose changes to programs, with an evolutionary process that keeps the promising ideas, discards the bad ones, and builds on what works. The evaluator keeps everything grounded. The language model can be as imaginative as it likes, but every idea gets tested against an objective measure.

Because of that design, we've been able to apply it to a remarkably diverse set of problems. On the mathematical side, it found a way to multiply four-by-four complex-valued matrices using 48 scalar multiplications, improving on Strassen's algorithm from 1969 for that setting. We gave it a broad collection of open problems in analysis, geometry, and combinatorics, and in most cases it matched the best known constructions, and in a meaningful fraction it improved on them. Then on the very practical side, it found a scheduling heuristic for Google's data centers that recovers a small but significant fraction of our fleet-wide compute. It sped up kernels used in training Gemini itself, and it proposed simplifications to circuit designs for TPUs.

So you go from pure mathematics to data center operations to hardware design with essentially the same system. That's what excites me.

But I want to be clear about the boundaries, because they matter. The generality is bounded by the evaluator. If you can't write down what "better" means in a way a machine can check, AlphaEvolve struggles. A lot of important science doesn't fit that mold yet. You might need a wet-lab experiment that takes weeks, or the quality of a solution might involve human judgment that's hard to formalize. So part of the research frontier is expanding the set of problems we can bring into this framework, whether through better simulators, learned evaluators, or tighter integration with real experiments.

The way I'd summarize it: AlphaEvolve is general across any domain where discovery can be framed as searching over programs with a measurable objective. That turns out to cover far more of science, mathematics, and engineering than people might initially assume. And as the underlying models improve, the system improves too, so I think we're still early in understanding how far that generality really reaches.

r001.rationale: It describes AlphaEvolve finding a matrix-multiplication method that improves on Strassen’s algorithm, supporting the claim that it can discover algorithms.

r002.rationale: It says solutions must be expressible as code, but does not identify searching across different programming-language representations as part of AlphaEvolve’s generality.

r003.rationale: It requires automatic evaluation and says candidate ideas are tested, but does not state that the evaluator can score them quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that surprised us most was how broad it turned out to be. When we started, the honest expectation was that we were building a tool for a fairly narrow class of problems, things where you can write down a scoring function, hand it to the system, and let it search over programs. And that's still the core of it. AlphaEvolve needs an automated evaluator. If you can't tell it whether one candidate is better than another, it can't do much for you.

But what we underestimated was how many problems fit that description once you look carefully. We applied it to open questions in mathematics, things like the kissing number in eleven dimensions, or constructions for matrix multiplication, where it found a faster algorithm for four by four complex matrices than Strassen's from the 1960s. And then, the same system, with essentially no changes, we pointed at our own infrastructure. Scheduling in Borg, our data center orchestration system, where it found a heuristic that recovered on the order of point seven percent of Google's compute fleet. Kernel optimization for Gemini training. Even parts of the TPU circuit design.

So the generality isn't that it understands every domain. It's that the loop is domain-agnostic. You have an LLM proposing code changes, you have an evaluator giving a signal, and you have an evolutionary process keeping the promising ideas and discarding the rest. The language model brings in the broad prior knowledge, the evaluator brings in the rigor, and evolution ties them together.

Where I'd put the boundary is this. It works brilliantly when verification is cheap and reliable. It struggles when the evaluation itself is the hard part, when you need a human to judge, or an expensive physical experiment, or when the metric is a poor proxy for what you actually care about. Those are the problems we're most interested in pushing on next, because that's where a lot of real science lives.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve found a faster algorithm for 4×4 complex matrix multiplication, describing a newly discovered algorithm.

r002.rationale: It describes searching over programs and applying the system across domains, but does not identify searching across different programming-language representations.

r003.rationale: It says an automated evaluator must compare candidates and that verification should be cheap and reliable, but does not clearly state that candidate proposals must be scored quickly.

astra-6.text:
I think the key to understanding AlphaEvolve’s generality is to ask: can you express the problem in code, and can you evaluate whether a proposed solution is better? If you can do those two things, then you have the ingredients for applying this approach.

The system proposes changes to an algorithm, evaluates them, and uses that feedback to search for better solutions. That gives it a broad scope, because many different problems share that structure, even when the underlying domains look very different.

But there is an important qualification: it depends on the evaluator. If success is difficult to measure, or evaluating a candidate is prohibitively expensive, then applying the system becomes much harder. So I would describe it as a general approach to algorithm discovery and optimization, with the ability to evaluate solutions being the central constraint.

r001.rationale: The response describes algorithm discovery and optimization, but does not clearly say AlphaEvolve can discover entirely new algorithms.

r002.rationale: It does not identify searching across different programming-language representations as part of AlphaEvolve’s generality.

r003.rationale: It says application depends on an evaluator and becomes harder when evaluating candidates is prohibitively expensive, communicating that candidate evaluation must be efficient.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish generality across problems from generality across every kind of task. AlphaEvolve is general in the sense that it isn’t designed around one particular mathematical problem or one particular algorithm. You can give it different problems, and it can search for programs that improve on the solutions you already have.

But there’s an important condition: you need a way to evaluate those programs. Can you check that a candidate is correct, and can you measure whether it’s better? That feedback is what allows the system to make progress. So I would describe its scope as broad within problems where you can express a solution in code and evaluate it reliably. That’s a very substantial space, but it isn’t the same as saying it can solve any problem.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaEvolve can search for programs that improve existing solutions, but does not clearly state that it can discover entirely new algorithms.

r002.rationale: It mentions expressing solutions in code, but does not identify searching across different programming-language representations as a dimension of generality.

r003.rationale: It says candidate programs need to be checked for correctness and measured for improvement, but does not state that the evaluator must score proposals quickly.
